title: Darjeeling and Kalimpong on a budget
meta_description: Darjeeling on a budget in 2026: real costs for trains, shared jeeps, lodges, homestays, food and the toy train, with sample 3- and 6-night budgets.
summary: You can see Darjeeling and Kalimpong for about ₹2,000–3,500 per person a day in 2026. Take an overnight train to New Jalpaiguri, shared jeeps between towns, government lodges and homestays, and local cafes. Spend on the toy train, Tiger Hill and a good tea, and save everywhere else.

sections.heading: What a day really costs
paras: The Darjeeling hills are one of the cheapest parts of the Himalaya to reach and to travel in. The railhead at New Jalpaiguri is only three hours from Darjeeling by road, shared jeeps link every town, and there are government lodges and homestays at every stop. A careful traveller sharing a room can spend about ₹2,000–3,500 a day on the ground, including a bed, two or three meals and local transport.

The table below shows what travellers pay locally in 2026. These are indicative ranges per person unless marked, and they rise in peak weeks: April to early June, the Durga Puja and Dashain weeks, and Christmas to New Year. Fares and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Getting there for less
paras: The biggest saving is the journey up. From Kolkata, overnight trains such as the Darjeeling Mail and Padatik Express leave Sealdah in the evening and reach New Jalpaiguri (NJP) in the morning. A sleeper berth costs about ₹500–700 and saves you a hotel night. Book 60 days ahead for holiday weekends, when berths go in minutes. From Delhi, trains to NJP take a day or more; compare with a flight to Bagdogra, which can be cheaper when booked early.

At NJP, ignore the touts on the platform and walk out to the jeep stand. Shared jeeps leave for Darjeeling, Kalimpong and Mirik when full, and the per-seat price is usually written on a board or quoted at a counter. A reserved car to Darjeeling costs about ₹3,000–4,000, which only makes sense for a group of four or more. If you fly into Bagdogra, take a cheap taxi or auto to Siliguri, about 12 km, and catch a shared jeep there.

sections.heading: Moving around by shared jeep
paras: Shared jeeps are how local people travel, and they will be your main transport. Each town has a motor stand: in Darjeeling it is the stand below Chowk Bazaar, in Kalimpong the main motor stand in town. Jeeps carry up to ten people, run mostly in the morning, and leave when every seat is sold. Buy your seat early, sit in the middle row if you want a little more space, and keep a light bag on your lap.

Some routes need a change. For Lava and Rishyap, go to Kalimpong first. For Sittong and Takdah, shared jeeps are few, and a short reserved car from Kurseong or Darjeeling is often the practical choice; split it with other travellers. NBSTC buses run between Siliguri and the hill towns and are cheaper than jeeps but slower and less frequent.
list: Be at the jeep stand by 7–8 am for long transfers; afternoon jeeps are rare.
Ask the counter for the next departure before you buy a seat, so you are not waiting for hours.
Pay a little more for the front seat if you get motion sickness.
Book the return jeep to NJP the evening before on busy days.

sections.heading: Sleeping cheap but well
paras: Government lodges are the backbone of a budget trip here. The West Bengal Tourism Development Corporation runs Meghbalika in Darjeeling and Roudra Chhaya in Kurseong, and the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation runs the forest cottages at Lava. Rooms are simple, clean enough and fairly priced, and you can book them online through the state portals. Darjeeling also has many small family hotels below Chowrasta; walk in and ask in the shoulder months.

Homestays are the best value in the villages. In Sittong, Rishyap, Takdah, Lava and Lepchajagat, families charge about ₹1,500–2,500 per person including dinner and breakfast. That is cheaper than a town hotel once you count meals, and you eat home-cooked food. Bathrooms may be shared and hot water may come in a bucket; ask before you book. Most budget rooms in the hills have no heating, so pack thermals from November to February rather than paying for a room heater.

sections.heading: Eating well for ₹500 a day
paras: Food is cheap if you eat where locals do. A plate of momos or a bowl of thukpa costs ₹80–180 in a cafe off the Mall, and a full thali or rice meal ₹150–300. The lanes around Chowk Bazaar and Laden La Road in Darjeeling, and the area around the haat in Kalimpong, are cheaper than the Mall and Chowrasta. Sel roti and aloo dum from roadside stalls make a filling breakfast.

Tea is the one thing worth spending on. A cup of good first flush at a tasting counter costs more than the milky tea at a stall, but it is the taste of the place. Buy loose tea only from shops that name the estate and flush. Bottled water adds up; carry a bottle and refill at your lodge where filtered water is available, which also cuts plastic on the hills.

sections.heading: Sample budgets for two trips
paras: Here is what two of our saver journeys cost per person, twin sharing, on the ground, excluding trains to NJP. A long weekend in Darjeeling from Kolkata, three nights, comes to about ₹9,500 with a budget lodge and breakfast, shared jeeps, Tiger Hill and the diesel joy ride. Six nights across Darjeeling, Kalimpong, Lava and Rishyap comes to about ₹17,500 with breakfast and dinner on most days.

Solo travellers pay more, because single rooms cost nearly as much as doubles. Students can cut costs further with dormitory beds where hostels operate and by skipping the joy ride. The money you save on transport and rooms is best spent on one splurge: the steam toy train, a night at Morgan House in Kalimpong, or a guided Sandakphu trek.

sections.heading: Six ways to spend less
list: Travel in early March, late November or the first half of December, when Darjeeling hotels cut rates and views are often good.
Take the diesel joy ride instead of steam; it runs the same loop to Ghum and Batasia.
Share a Tiger Hill jeep with other guests rather than booking a private car.
Use homestays with meals in villages; dinner and breakfast are included in the price.
Avoid the Durga Puja week and the last ten days of December unless you book months ahead.
Walk: Darjeeling's sights, from Observatory Hill to Happy Valley, are close together if you can manage slopes.
paras: Money is easy to manage. Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik and Kalimpong all have ATMs and most shops take UPI. Carry cash for Lava, Rishyap, Sittong and Takdah, where network can fail and homestays often prefer cash.

faqs.q: How much does a Darjeeling trip cost per person on a budget?
faqs.a: About ₹2,000–3,500 per person a day in 2026, sharing a room, for a government lodge or homestay, local meals and shared jeeps. A three-night long weekend from Kolkata costs about ₹9,500 on the ground plus the train. Prices rise in April–June, Puja week and Christmas.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to get from NJP to Darjeeling?
faqs.a: A shared jeep from outside NJP station, about ₹250–400 a seat and 3–3.5 hours. NBSTC buses from Siliguri's Tenzing Norgay Bus Terminus are slightly cheaper but slower and less frequent. The toy train from NJP is slow and costs more.

faqs.q: Are government lodges in Darjeeling good value?
faqs.a: Yes, for budget travellers. WBTDC's Meghbalika in Darjeeling and Roudra Chhaya in Kurseong offer simple, fairly priced rooms close to the centre, bookable online. They are plain and may be unheated, but clean and well located. Book early for peak weeks.

faqs.q: How much is a homestay in the Darjeeling villages?
faqs.a: About ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night in 2026, including dinner and breakfast, in villages such as Sittong, Rishyap, Takdah and Lepchajagat. Rooms are simple; some share bathrooms. It is often cheaper than a town hotel once meals are counted.

faqs.q: Is the toy train worth it on a budget?
faqs.a: The two-hour joy ride to Ghum and back is worth it for most visitors. Diesel costs about ₹1,000 and steam about ₹1,500–1,700. Choose diesel to save money; the route and views are the same. Book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can students do Darjeeling for under ₹10,000?
faqs.a: Yes. Three nights with sleeper trains, shared jeeps, a budget lodge or dormitory, local food and the diesel joy ride can come in under ₹10,000 including the train, if you share a room and avoid peak weeks.

January, February and July to August are cheapest, but the monsoon months bring rain and landslides. The best value is early March, late November and early December, when rates drop and views are often clear.

faqs.q: Do I need cash in Darjeeling?
faqs.a: In towns, UPI and cards work widely and there are ATMs in Darjeeling, Kurseong, Mirik and Kalimpong. In villages such as Lava, Rishyap, Sittong and Takdah, carry cash, since network is patchy and ATMs are few or absent.

Yes, in a small group. Guide fees, lodges, park entry and meals come to roughly ₹10,000–16,000 per person for four to five days from Manebhanjan. A guide is required in Singalila National Park. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.
